summary: The legacy book has 14 interactive geometry experiences in two generations, plus shared math-typesetting and fallback tools. The newer 'Geometry Lab 01–05' series was built 9–10 Sep 2026 (commits 230ab25, 2fc1cde, c3d5533, 64cc990, b257fd8): polar coordinates (§4.2), comparing a vector field at two points (§6.1), flow order and the Lie bracket (§6.6), continuous parallel transport on a plane, cylinder and sphere (§7.1), and two routes to one endpoint (opening Ch. 8). It shares one look and one saved-state format. Four more labs have their own looks: a curved surface with two overlapping charts (Ch. 4), Mercury's perihelion precession (§16.6), counting the independent Riemann components (Ch. 8) and a tidal particle cloud (§9.3). The older 'visual arguments' (commit 0e8afcc) cover stereographic charts, a polar metric cell, a rotating polar basis, octant transport in four steps, and horizon light directions (§17). The new series largely replaced them, but they stayed in the book, so Chapters 4, 6 and 8 show two different interfaces for the same idea. The mathematics is unusually careful. Each model is checked against an independent method: RK4 integration of the transport equation, Simpson quadrature, integrated flows, all 256 Riemann symmetry/Bianchi cases, and exact geodesic-deviation (Jacobi) solutions. The five suites with a model-only mode (check-flow-order, check-parallel-transport, check-vector-fields and check-geometry-foundations with --models; check-curvature-experiences with --unit-only) were re-run on 2026-09-12 and all exit 0. check-geometry-experiences.mjs and check-visual-lessons.mjs have no model-only flag: their numerical asserts run first in the same process, which then launches Playwright against a local build. Playwright checks cover 390/1440 px in both themes, overflow, label bounds, saved state, pausing offscreen, WebGL context loss and no-JavaScript fallbacks. The best assets are the parallel-transport pair (exact model, antialiased grid painted in the shader on one surface mesh, fixed-scale orthographic camera, face-on view) and the vector-field product-rule lab. The weaknesses are four different interface shells, two ways of labelling math (SVG text vs KaTeX), duplicated concepts, preset-only controls in the older lessons, and several planned items never built: a toggle between unit and coordinate basis vectors, moving markers and a flux box for divergence, an unrolled cylinder view, a shaded loop area, and R(X,Y)V. Geometry Labs 01–05 publish machine-readable state (data-scientific-context: model, parameters, readouts, units, assumptions, equations) plus narration text describing the current state. The manifold, precession, Riemann-count, tidal-cloud and older visual-lesson labs publish only data-narration-source and data-visual-state, which web/scientific-context.js reads as a fallback. The manifold, precession, Riemann-count and tidal-cloud labs also do not save state across reloads (their get/restore functions are called only by the Playwright checks). That is almost exactly what a GPT-Live tutor needs and should become a typed contract in grbook.ai.
lessons_learned: Keep the independent-numerics check pattern. Each model was checked by a different method: RK4 integration of dV/ds = −(V·dn/ds)n along a straight-chord parametrisation against exact great-circle rotations (check-parallel-transport.mjs), Simpson quadrature of analytic field derivatives (check-vector-fields.mjs), step-by-step integration of the flows (check-flow-order.mjs), all 256 index combinations for the Riemann symmetries and cyclic identity (check-curvature-experiences.mjs), and the null condition in ingoing Eddington–Finkelstein coordinates (check-visual-lessons.mjs). The five suites with a --models/--unit-only flag passed on 2026-09-12. The geometry-experiences and visual-lessons checks mix numerics and Playwright in one run, so their numerics cannot run in CI without a browser. Split them. Port them as Vitest unit tests next to each Svelte lab.

Make the state contract a typed interface from day one. The legacy labs publish data-visual-state, data-narration-source (text describing the current state, with TeX), data-scientific-context JSON {model, parameters, readouts, units, assumptions, equations}, and a gr:visual-change event. That gives the voice tutor grounded, current numbers without screen-scraping. In the legacy code it was re-implemented ad hoc in each file, and web/geometry-experiences.js, web/curvature-experiences.js and web/visual-lessons.js do not emit scientificContext at all. The consumer, web/scientific-context.js visibleExperiments(), therefore takes up to two visible lab roots and falls back to scraping up to 6,000 characters of visible p/li/output text plus every visible range, select, pressed button and tab. A typed contract removes the need to scrape.

Design one lab shell and one labelling system before building labs. The legacy book has four shells: a card with a serif h2 and 'GEOMETRY LAB / 0n' eyebrow, the gx-* layout (no card, sans title), cx-* (no card, bold sans), and vl-* (tinted card, 9–12 px text). It has two saved-state keys (gr-course-v1 and gr-visual-lessons:v1). It labels math two ways: plain SVG text such as 'eθ', 'Δθ', 'h²' in the polar, field and flow labs, versus KaTeX overlays positioned from the SVG's screen transform elsewhere. check-geometry-experiences.mjs asserts that no SVG text exists, yet the Geometry Lab series relies on it.

Retire superseded interfaces. The five older visual lessons (charts, metric, basis, transport) repeat concepts that the newer Geometry Labs teach better, yet both were kept, so readers learn two interfaces for coordinates, moving bases and transport. docs/visual-development-plan-2026-09-09.md §3 itself warns against this. It also judged four discrete transport states and a basis rotating at one point insufficient.

Continuous parameters beat presets. What worked was a scrub slider plus a play button, 'Next corner' stepping, a reverse control, a size control that shrinks the loop toward its start, and a radius control that separates angular size from physical area. Opening in a state that already shows the effect also worked: the routes lab starts on the completed sphere with 90° visible. The older lessons' five-point and three-radius presets felt like a slideshow.

3D technique worth copying: paint grids and chart patches in the fragment shader with fwidth antialiasing instead of drawing coincident line meshes, which caused z-fighting and flicker (see parallel-transport-scene.js makeSurface and geometry-experiences.js initSpatial). Fit the camera to a bounding sphere once per resize, not per drag, so the model does not appear to 'breathe'. Use an orthographic camera with a fixed frustum when angles are measured. Give every measurement scene a 'look straight at' button. Recreate OrbitControls after changing camera.up.

Theme pitfall found only by eye: passing the luminous dark-theme text colour into a lit surface material washed out the sphere and the blue route (docs/parallel-transport-review.md, 'Dark-theme surface repair'). Surface-colour tokens must be separate from text and marker tokens, and unlit teaching marks should skip tone mapping so they match the legend.

Screenshot review caught what assertions missed: an overlit surface, camera fits that left models too small, labels colliding on phones, and a horizon cone too small inside the horizon (geometry-experiences-review.md, visual-lessons-review.md, visualization-audit.md). Keep a human screenshot review at 390 and 1440 px in both themes as a release gate.

Lifecycle bugs to design out: IntersectionObserver batches can deliver a stale hidden entry first, so use entries.at(-1). This bug surfaced only on reload and has a dedicated regression test. On resume, never integrate the wall-clock time that passed while hidden (the cloud check asserts the jump is at most 0.006). Never auto-start animation; respect reduced motion but still allow an explicit Play. After a WebGL context loss, redraw the current state immediately as SVG and disable camera-only buttons.

Honest model disclosures should be kept and fed to the tutor. Examples: the precessing Kepler ellipse with only the extra angle magnified 300,000×, 'not an exact Schwarzschild geodesic'; the cloud's 'not a universal Ricci/Weyl decomposition'; flow order 'not a fluid or physical clock'; 'finite projection is not exact transport'. Each lab has a 'model and its limits' disclosure; in grbook.ai these belong in the knowledge vault so the voice tutor repeats the same caveats.

Planned but never built (docs/visual-development-plan-2026-09-09.md §3; treat as backlog): a toggle between unit and coordinate basis vectors (∂θ = r ê_θ) drawn on the polar grid; mapping a coordinate rectangle to a physical area patch (determinant / volume element); moving markers plus a flux box in the vector-field lab; the limit P_{γ(h)→p} V − V → ∇_X V; an unrolled companion view of the cylinder; a shaded enclosed region with an orientation arrow; two transported vectors showing their inner product is preserved; R(X,Y)V built from two orders of displacement; holonomy on a loop that cannot be shrunk to a point.

The semantic colouring in scripts/math-system.mjs guesses roles from letters and hard-coded chapter-number regexes (for example /^(8|9|10|12|…)$/). It cannot transfer to a new curriculum. Keep the idea (colour the geometric object, never indices; five roles: geometry, transport, curvature, matter, observer) but author semantic TeX macros explicitly, keyed to concept-registry ids.

Good placement habit: when a lab replaces a static figure (chapterFigure in build-site.mjs), the old figure stays available as an optional 'reference diagram'. Labs are inserted with explicit markers in the prose and appear after the terms they use are defined, before the formula they motivate. Keep both rules in the grbook.ai lesson schema.

Preview must never be the same as commit. The Riemann-count lab calls pairSelect(r, c) on pointermove, which rewrites data-narration-source and data-visual-state for whichever tile is under the cursor; pointerout then republishes the committed tile. A tutor reading state mid-hover would describe a tile the learner never chose. In grbook.ai, emit tutor events only for committed selections and keep hover as local UI state.

One sign convention per quantity, shown the same everywhere. In the transport labs the face-on arc label prints Math.abs(angle) ('90.0°', parallel-transport-scene.js:122) while the readout and insight text print the signed '−90.0°' (routes-sphere-1440-light.png). Readers and the tutor see two values for one angle. Show the sign in both places, with an orientation arrow that explains it.

Saving state has to be a platform feature, not something each lab opts into. Only the Geometry Labs (gr-course-v1) and the older visual lessons (gr-visual-lessons:v1) persist. The manifold, precession, Riemann-count and tidal-cloud labs export get/restore functions that nothing in production calls, so their state resets on every reload.

assets.title: Geometry Lab 01 — One point. Two addresses. (polar coordinates, arc vs chord)
assets.teaches: The same point on a flat plane has Cartesian (x, y) and polar (r, θ) addresses, both in metres/radians. The angle is undefined at the origin even though the plane is regular there, so a coordinate failure is not a failure of the geometry. A fixed angular step Δθ sweeps an arc rθ·Δθ that grows with r. The straight chord 2r·sin(Δθ/2) is shorter for a finite step, and the two agree as Δθ → 0. This is the angular term of the polar metric.
assets.pedagogy: Picture first, formula later: it appears before the first polar transformation in §4.2, and §4.5 returns to it before deriving ds² = dr² + r²dθ². Two views (Coordinates / An angular step). A short insight line changes with the state; it says so explicitly at the origin. A collapsible 'From the picture to a distance' derives the chord from the isosceles triangle and takes the small-angle limit. It states explicitly that curved coordinate lines do not make the plane curved.

controls: drag the point P on the plot (pointer capture, uses the SVG's screen transform)
Angular step Δθ slider 0.02–0.8 rad (step view only)
interaction.what_updates: The SVG redraws completely on each input: square and polar grids, radius segment, angle arc, projection guides, and in step view the swept sector, arc, chord and Q. The readouts, insight text, narration source and scientific-context JSON also update, and state is saved to localStorage gr-course-v1.
readouts: slider values, with 'Undefined' angle at the origin
interaction.rendering: Hand-built SVG strings; labels are SVG text with Unicode (θ, Δθ), not KaTeX. KaTeX only in the details text via math-system.mjs.

assets.physics_model: Euclidean plane: x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ; arc = rΔθ; chord = 2r sin(Δθ/2). Inputs are clamped and non-finite values fall back to defaults. Verified at 90 (r, θ, Δθ) combinations: |P| = r, chord equals the independently computed endpoint separation, arc ≥ chord, round trip through polarFromPoint, chord/arc → 1 at Δθ = 0.02, no NaN in the SVG. Browser checks: keyboard, drag, origin disabling, saved state, no-JS static SVG.

strengths: Clean, uncluttered plot with a sidebar at 1440 px and sensible stacking at 390 px (screenshots)
Handles the origin honestly: the angle slider is disabled and the text explains why
Shows arc vs chord numerically, which makes the metric's local character concrete
Narration and state contract updated on every change
issues: Plot labels are SVG text with Unicode, unlike the KaTeX-labelled labs
No unit vs coordinate basis arrows (∂θ = r ê_θ), which the ledger required (visual-development-plan §3 Experience A)
No area-element or determinant cell; ds² is never drawn on the actual displacement
Overlaps the older visual-lesson 'metric' cell in the same chapter

assets.title: Geometry Lab 02 — Compare two nearby arrows (component change vs frame change)
paths: book.md:1966 (§6.1 'A fixed arrow with changing components')
assets.teaches: Four steady plane fields (uniform, expansion, rotation, shear; rate 0.4/s) are sampled at P and Q on a circle of radius 1.8 m. In a uniform field the arrows are identical, yet their polar components differ. In rotation and expansion on the circle the components are constant, yet the arrows differ. The exact finite identity V_Q − V_P = B_P(c_Q − c_P) + (B_Q − B_P)c_Q splits the change into a component term and a frame term, drawn head to tail. Shrinking the separation leads toward the connection term.
assets.pedagogy: Designed around a paradox. The key insight changes with the chosen field; field samples are distinguished from particles, and the gold frame arrows from velocities. A details panel explains the matrix notation B, c before using it, and why the second term must use c_Q. Another states the limits: prescribed steady fields, comparison by Euclidean translation only, unit frame vs ∂θ = r ê_θ. It sets up the need for a transport rule on curved surfaces.

controls: field choice: Uniform / Expansion / Rotation / Shear
disclosure: component vs frame change (second comparison plot)
interaction.what_updates: Field quiver, the P and Q velocity arrows and unit frames, the route arc, the common-origin comparison plot (P, Q, difference), the head-to-tail decomposition plot, the numeric identity, polar components at P and Q, the insight text, narration and scientific context.
readouts: radial and tangential components at P and at Q [m/s]
interaction.rendering: SVG strings; labels are SVG text ('eᵣ', 'eθ' without hats); the formula in the details is KaTeX via math-system.

assets.physics_model: V_uniform = (1, 0) m/s; expansion k(x, y); rotation k(−y, x); shear k(y, 0); k = 0.4/s. Unit polar frame e_r = (cos θ, sin θ), e_θ = (−sin θ, cos θ). The finite decomposition is exact with no small-step approximation. Checked at 72 combinations: frame orthonormality, the decomposition summing to the difference, analytic components per field, and the difference against composite Simpson integration (n = 128) of analytic d/dθ along the circle. Browser: all fields, keyboard, saved state, no-JS static view.

strengths: Pedagogically the sharpest idea in this group: constant components with a changing vector, and the reverse
The exact finite product rule is shown geometrically, not just asserted
The common-origin inset makes 'compare after translation' visible
Mathematically verified by independent quadrature
issues: The main field plot is small and busy at 1440 px: P, Q, frames and the 'eθ' label crowd one small region (field-rotation-1440-dark.png)
SVG labels are un-hatted Unicode while the text uses ê_θ
The most important construction (component + frame) is hidden in a collapsed details panel
No moving markers, divergence flux box or coordinate-basis mode (ledger Experience B not met)
A 'separation → 0' limit readout (divide by Δθ) is promised but not shown

assets.title: Geometry Lab 04 — Try the other order (flows and the Lie bracket)
paths: book.md:2231 (§6.6 'When the order of two flows matters')
assets.teaches: Follow X = (1, 0) then Y = (0, x) from P = (1, 0) for the same parameter h, and compare with Y then X. The endpoints (1+h, h+h²) and (1+h, h) differ by h² vertically. Dividing by h² gives the bracket [X, Y] = (0, 1). The gap comes from Y's instruction varying with position, not from curvature or torsion; the plane is flat.
assets.pedagogy: Added after a review found §7.2 used the Lie bracket untaught and cited a nonexistent example. The picture precedes the bracket formula. Playback shows the two moves; outlined final markers stay as references. The insight says to shrink h and watch the gap scale as h². A details panel derives h(1+h) − h = h² and contrasts endpoint mismatch with the direction mismatch of parallel transport.

interaction.what_updates: Both route polylines (planned dashed plus travelled), moving dots, endpoint markers A/B, the h² bracket annotation, the gap readout, narration and scientific context.
interaction.rendering: SVG strings; SVG text labels ('h²', 'P = (1, 0)'); KaTeX in the details text.

assets.physics_model: Exact flows: X shifts x at unit rate; Y raises y at rate x. Dimensionless coordinates and parameter. The model is verified against 256-step integration of each field in both orders, h² scaling and continuity between stages. Browser: three step sizes, keyboard, playback, saved state, aligned sliders on phones, no-JS view.

strengths: Minimal, readable construction; the h² bracket annotation is clear
Explicitly guards against 'noncommuting implies curvature or torsion'
Fills a real prerequisite gap found by review
issues: 'Gap divided by h²' is a string literal, not computed; for this exact example it is always 1, so the O(h³) character of the general case is never seen
Shows two routes, not the standard four-leg commutator loop
Only one field pair; no second example where the bracket varies with position
Plain SVG text labels

assets.title: Geometry Lab 03 — Carry an arrow home (continuous parallel transport on plane, cylinder, sphere)
paths: book.md:2289 (§7.1 'Parallel transport along a path'; revisited in §8.3)
assets.teaches: Moving an arrow without twisting it within the tangent plane keeps it constant on a plane. On a rolled sheet (cylinder) it changes direction in the room yet returns unrotated, because the sheet is intrinsically flat. On a sphere it returns rotated after a geodesic triangle: −90° for the octant. The rotation shrinks with loop size, flips sign when the route is reversed, and equals K × signed area with K = 1/R². At fixed angular size a larger radius gives more area but the same angle. The surface rule dV/ds = −(V·dn/ds)n preserves length.
assets.pedagogy: Sequence: plane, then rolled sheet, then sphere, with the term 'great circle' defined before use. The readout reports the rotation 'on return' even mid-journey, rather than a misleading partial value. 'Look straight at A' removes foreshortening. The details derive the transport rule from differentiating the tangency condition V·n = 0, then explain the exact checks. They name corners as places where the path turns but the arrow does not, and define Gaussian curvature as return rotation per unit area in the small-loop limit.

controls: Play/Pause/Replay (9 s per circuit, pauses offscreen)
Surface radius slider 0.8–1.6 m (hidden for the plane)
orbit by drag or arrow keys, Home resets
interaction.what_updates: Moving arrow and marker, a tangent-plane patch oriented to (V, n × V, n), a smaller reference arrow at the start, tube routes for three legs, vertex labels hidden when occluded (raycast), and the surface mesh rebuilt when surface, radius, size or reverse change. Readouts, insight, narration and scientific context update; a projection dataset supports tests. The SVG fallback redraws when WebGL is unavailable.
interaction.rendering: three.js WebGLRenderer, orthographic camera with fixed frustum, ACES tone mapping, MeshStandardMaterial surface with a grid injected into the shader (fwidth antialiasing), TubeGeometry routes, cylinder+cone arrows, HTML labels projected from 3D. Static fallback: a painter-sorted, faceted SVG surface with dashed far-side paths.

assets.physics_model: Exact Levi-Civita transport for the induced Euclidean metric. Plane: constant vector. Cylinder: constant components in the unrolled frame, mapped through the embedding (R sin(u/R), v, R(1 − cos(u/R))). Sphere: each leg is a great-circle rotation (Rodrigues) of both point and vector about cross(A, B); no projection or renormalisation. Signed area on the sphere comes from the solid-angle formula 2R²·atan2(A·(B×C), 1 + A·B + B·C + C·A). The angle is measured with the outward-normal right-hand rule. Verified over 54 configurations: unit length and tangency at 41 samples, closure, angle = K·signed area, octant |angle| = π/2, area = R²(2·corner − π/2), 512-step RK4 of dV/dt = −(V·dn/dt)n along a normalised chord (a different parametrisation) matching to 4e-10, and retracing the route restores the start vector. Browser: face-on projected perpendicularity, fixed frustum while orbiting, playback pause offscreen, saved state, context loss redrawing the current state, no-JS.

strengths: Exact model with independent numerical verification; the gold standard in this group
Beautiful, legible sphere and cylinder in both themes after the dark-surface repair (screenshots)
Face-on view and fixed-scale orthographic camera keep the camera from creating the rotation being measured
Controls expose the three variables that matter (size, radius, orientation)
Robust lifecycle: offscreen pause, reduced motion, context loss, saved state
issues: The enclosed region is not shaded and the orientation of the loop is not shown in 3D; the sign convention lives only in the details
The cylinder has no unrolled companion view, so 'intrinsically flat' is only asserted

Arrows are small relative to the sphere at 1440 px; the A label and tangent patch overlap in the default view; in light theme the tangent-plane patch at A shows as a beige square sticking out past the sphere's silhouette, and the red carried arrow is short (transport-sphere-1440-light.png)
No second transported vector to show inner products are preserved; no noncontractible loop around the cylinder
Default plane surface opens on the least surprising case
Rotation readout is signed ('−90.0°') with the right-hand-rule convention explained only in the collapsed details

assets.title: Geometry Lab 05 — Two routes. One destination. (path dependence of transport)
paths: web/parallel-transport-scene.js (routes=true: direct marker, direct tangent patch, angle arc)
docs/parallel-transport-review.md#Two prescribed routes to a common endpoint
assets.teaches: Two identical arrows start at A. One goes directly to C and one via B, both with the no-twist rule. On the sphere they meet at C differing by 90° for the octant; on the plane and cylinder they agree. Following one route out and the other back forms a loop, so the mismatch at C equals the loop's return rotation. Smaller triangles give smaller angles; the angle depends on angular size, not on radius.
assets.pedagogy: Opens Chapter 8 already completed on the sphere, so the effect is visible at once. It is distinguished explicitly from the Chapter 6 two-flow experiment, whose endpoints differ. Directions are compared only where both vectors share a tangent plane. Progress is a fraction of each route length, not a physical speed. 'Look straight at C' shows a gold angle arc labelled in degrees.

controls: Back to A / Meet at C
orbit by drag or arrows, Home
interaction.what_updates: Blue direct and pink via-B arrows and routes, a tangent patch at the direct arrow, and at completion a gold angle arc plus a degree label. Readouts, narration and context update as in lab 03.
readouts: angle when they meet at C [deg]
interaction.rendering: Same three.js scene as lab 03 with routes = true; SVG fallback from a viewpoint where C is visible.

assets.physics_model: Uses the same exact kernel as the loop. Direct leg is the great-circle rotation from A to C. Verified over 27 configurations: RK4 along both routes matches the analytic vectors to 4e-10, endpoints coincide, unit length and tangency throughout, and the angle equals the closed-loop holonomy. Browser: stale IntersectionObserver entries injected to regression-test 3D loading, face-on perpendicularity with the '90.0°' label visible, fixed frustum, playback, saved state.

strengths: The face-on angle arc is an unusually clear depiction of path dependence (routes-face-on-1440.png)
The default state shows the result immediately
Numerically tied to the loop result, which gives a natural bridge from holonomy to curvature

The degree label can crowd the arrowheads in the oblique default view (routes-sphere-1440-light.png)

assets.title: A curved world. A flat address. (surface, two overlapping charts, tangent plane)
paths: scripts/build-site.mjs:178 (inserted before guided lesson 'two-maps-one-sphere' in Chapter 4)
assets.teaches: A point on a curved 2D surface needs only two numbers. A chart assigns coordinates on an open disk; a flat map disk corresponds to a patch on the surface. Switching between overlapping charts A (u, v) and B (u′, v′) changes the numbers but not the point. A chart that does not cover a point says so rather than inventing coordinates. The tangent plane is the first-order approximation at a point.
assets.pedagogy: The deck invites the reader to move a point between the surface and its map, then change the map. The insight text distinguishes three cases: covered by both charts, by one, or by neither. The model details give F_A, the height function, the rotation-plus-translation transition, why the charts are full rank, and the honest caveat that this graph also admits a global chart and the faded rim is a render window.

controls: drag or click in the flat map (clamped inside the disk)
arrow keys in the map (Shift for larger steps), Home returns to the overlap point
On the overlap / Outside the other chart shortcuts
orbit the surface by drag or arrows, Home

assets.title: Watch shape and volume part company (freely falling particle cloud, isotropic vs trace-free tide)
topics: expansion and shear of a geodesic congruence
assets.teaches: A small ball of particles released at rest in a freely falling frame evolves as ξ'' = Aξ with A = −c²𝓔, where 𝓔_ij = R_î0ĵ0. Isotropic focusing (−1, −1, −1) shrinks the volume while keeping the sphere round. A trace-free tide (2, −1, −1) has zero initial volume acceleration, yet it stretches the cloud (axis ratio about 3.1 at s = 0.9) and still reduces the volume later: V/V₀ = cosh(√2·s)·cos²s = 1 − s⁴/2 + ….
